62.title: Do the AI judges' sentence labels agree with a person's?
62.description: The author was to label 404 saved sentences blind, twice, to check six AI judges. That is not possible, so no pass or fail can be given. We report what the judges show without a reference, and how they respond to human-marked uncertainty words.
62.size: AI judging done, no person's labels, judge-only figures to come
62.why: Most of the project's caveat counts come from two AI judges labeling sentences, with a caveat counted only when both flag it. A review in October 2026 found that the two agree little beyond what luck would give, and that no label had ever been compared with a person's. Until that comparison is made, every count that uses the method is provisional. This cell makes the comparison. It also tries four more judges, to see whether some other rule for combining judges would do better.

expectations.text: The person's two rounds of labels, a week apart, would agree well beyond chance for each of the three kinds of caveat.
expectations.note: Cannot be tested: the author's labels, the reference this needed, are not available (noted 2 October 2026).

expectations.text: The method used so far, counting a caveat only when both original judges flag it, would match the person's labels well for all three kinds of caveat.
expectations.note: Cannot be tested: the author's labels, the reference this needed, are not available (noted 2 October 2026).

expectations.text: Some rule for combining the six judges, chosen on half of the sentences, would match the person's labels well on the other half.
expectations.note: Cannot be tested: the author's labels, the reference this needed, are not available (noted 2 October 2026).

expectations.text: We would report how each judge and each rule compares with the person, how judges compare with each other, and whether a judge repeats its own earlier label.
expectations.note: Reported without a pass/fail test, in the parts that need no person's labels, plus a public-collection check.

62.found: The six AI judges finished labeling the 404 sentences on 1 October 2026. The plan needed the author's own labels, twice a week apart, as the reference. On 2 October 2026 that turned out not to be possible, so we wrote down what can still be measured. That is how far the six judges agree with each other on each kind of caveat, and how far the two original judges agree with their own earlier labels. We also estimate each judge's accuracy in a way that assumes they err independently. We also check them on 400 product-review sentences from a public collection where people marked words of uncertainty. That last check is reported without a pass mark, because that collection marks uncertainty in general and our judges look for stated conditions, which is not the same thing. None of this can validate the caveat counts, which stay provisional.
62.means: Without a person's labels, the project cannot say whether its caveat counts are right, and the paper says so. The counts in Cells 30, 38, 41 and 46 stay provisional. The judge-only figures show how much the judges disagree among themselves, which bounds how far any count can be trusted.

10047.label: Plan
10047.title: Compare the AI judges with one person's blind labels
10047.summary: A sample of 404 saved sentences, half flagged by at least one of the two original judges and half by neither. The author labels each one twice, a week apart, seeing only the sentence. Six AI judges label the same sentences. The current method and twelve other ways of combining judges are then scored against the person's first round.

10759.label: Note
10759.title: The six AI judges have labeled the sentences
10759.summary: The six AI judges finished labeling the 404 sentences on 1 October 2026. Nothing is scored until the author's blind labels are finished and saved. The second round of labels can start a week after the first.

10775.label: Note
10775.title: Judging went cleanly, and when the plans became public
10775.summary: All six judges labeled all 404 sentences, with no unreadable replies. Nothing is counted from their labels until the author's own labels are saved. The plans for the new experiments were saved locally before any run and posted to the public repository 70 minutes before Cell 63 began. For this cell, the public posting came 50 minutes after the judging had started.

11265.label: Change to the plan
11265.title: No person's labels: what can still be measured
11265.summary: Written down on 2 October 2026 before the judges' labels were scored. The three expectations that needed the author's labels cannot be tested. Instead we report how far the six judges agree with each other and an estimate of their accuracy that needs no reference, plus how they respond to 400 review sentences with human-marked uncertainty cues from a public collection of reviews. The caveat counts stay provisional.

63.title: Does the editor catch a wrong figure it could check?
63.description: On 61 questions with computed answers, the editor never followed a note's wrong figure when the scenario stated the right one. When two notes disagreed it mostly used the first one listed and rarely told the reader. Two more editor models are still to run.
63.size: 610 runs with the main editor model
63.why: Cells 47 and 59 planted a value the editor could not check, and asked for it by name, so repeating it showed little. A review in October 2026 asked for a test where checking is possible. Here every question has a computed answer that changes when one input figure changes. In one setup the scenario itself states the right figure while a note quotes a wrong one, so the error can be caught. In others the figure appears only in the notes. Nothing tells the editor to include or check the figure.

expectations.text: With the right figure stated and quoted, the editor would answer correctly in at least 90% of runs. Otherwise the other results cannot be read.
expectations.note: Held up. With the right figure stated and quoted, the editor answered correctly in 119 of 122 runs (98%).

expectations.text: When a wrong figure in one note is the only source, the editor's answer would follow it in at least 80% of runs.
expectations.note: Held up. With a wrong figure in one note as the only source, the answer followed it in 112 of 122 runs (92%). The question text pointed the editor to the notes, so this mostly shows the setup worked.

expectations.text: When the scenario states the right figure, the editor would follow a note's wrong figure less often than when the note is the only source.
expectations.note: Held up. With the right figure in the scenario, the answer followed the note's wrong figure in 0 of 122 runs, against 112 of 122 when the note was the only source. No reply mentioned the mismatch.

expectations.text: When a second note quotes the right figure, the editor would follow the wrong figure less often than when the wrong note is the only source.
expectations.note: Held up, but the test was easy to pass. The wrong figure was followed in 62 of 122 runs (51%) instead of 92%, because the editor picked one of the two notes, usually the first one listed.

expectations.text: When two notes quote different figures, the editor's reply would mention both figures in fewer than half of runs.
expectations.note: Held up. Both figures appeared in 41 of 244 replies (17%). Averaged over the 14 kinds of question it was 19%, plausibly 9% to 29%. Our own read of 60 replies put the share that showed the disagreement near 1 in 5.

expectations.text: We would report which figure wins when two notes disagree, whether the order of the notes matters, and how often the editor gives some other answer or none.
expectations.note: Reported without a pass/fail test. The first note listed won in 170 of 244 runs (70%), and the larger figure in 133 of 226. Other answers were 2% to 8% of runs in each setup. Two runs of 610 gave no answer.

63.found:
The main editor model, gpt-oss-20B, finished 610 runs on 2 October 2026. With the right figure stated and quoted, it answered correctly in 119 of 122 runs (98%).

When a note misquoted a figure that the scenario itself stated, the answer never followed the note (0 of 122 runs). When the note was the only source, the answer followed its wrong figure in 112 of 122 runs (92%). No reply told the reader that a note disagreed with the scenario. The editor used the scenario's figure and said nothing, and it took no longer than usual.

When two notes gave different figures and the scenario gave none, the answer followed the first note listed in 170 of 244 runs (70%) and the second in 56. With one right and one wrong note, the wrong figure was followed in 62 of 122 runs (51%). Both figures appeared in 41 of 244 replies (17%). We read 60 of those replies ourselves to check the script's count. Counting replies that pointed out the disagreement without quoting both figures, about 1 in 5 let a reader see that two figures existed.

Three runs needed a second try, because the model used up its whole length allowance while thinking and returned nothing.
63.means: The editor does not pass on a note's wrong figure when the scenario states the right one. That is narrower than saying it catches errors. Nothing in its replies shows it noticed the mismatch. When the scenario is silent and two notes disagree, a second note helps only by chance. The editor picks one, usually the first, and in about 4 of 5 replies the reader is not told there was a choice. A design that relies on a second source needs a separate step that reports the disagreement. Cell 67 tests that in the full live system. The same 610 prompts still have to run on two other editor models.

10164.label: Plan
10164.title: Plant a wrong figure where it can and cannot be checked
10164.summary: Five setups per question: the right figure stated and quoted, a wrong figure quoted against the scenario, a wrong figure as the only source, a wrong and a right figure in two notes, and two different wrong figures. Two runs each on 61 questions, 610 runs per editor model. A script checks the final number against the computed answers.

10825.label: Result
10825.title: Runs finished: results by the rules set in advance
10825.summary: The main editor model finished its 610 runs on 2 October 2026. The clean-setup check passed and all four graded expectations held up, by the rules written down in advance. This entry holds the scoring script's output exactly as printed. Our reading of it is the next entry.

10856.label: Note
10856.title: What the result shows and what it does not
10856.summary: The editor used the scenario's figure over a misquoting note in every run, but never mentioned the mismatch. So we say it follows the scenario, and we do not say it catches errors. With two disagreeing notes it mostly took the first one listed, and about 1 reply in 5 let the reader see the disagreement. Three runs needed a second try. We read 60 replies ourselves to check the script's count.

64.title: Do other AI readers act on a caveat in the caveats section?
64.description: Six reader models read the reports from Cell 51 with a relevant or an irrelevant caveat in the attached section. We also remove the instruction that pointed at attachments and place the caveat among 4 or 9 real ones. Planned and queued to run.
64.size: Planned: 3,300 reads by six reader models
64.why: Cell 51 found that a reader model changed its decision when a relevant caveat sat in the attached section. A review in October 2026 named three limits. There were two readers, and one was the model that wrote the report. The reader's instruction told it to use anything attached. And the section held a single sentence, where real ones hold 5 to 53. This cell tests each limit, on the same 11 questions, with four readers that Cell 51 did not use.

expectations.text: With Cell 51's own setup, the four new reader models taken together would change their decision more often for the relevant caveat than for the irrelevant one.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. This is the main expectation of the cell.

expectations.text: Removing the instruction that points at attachments would reduce how much the relevant caveat changes decisions.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. The cell has not run.

expectations.text: Placing the relevant caveat among nine real caveats would reduce how much it changes decisions, compared with placing it alone.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. The cell has not run.

expectations.text: We would report each reader's results in each setup, the effect of where the caveat sits in the list, and how the two readers from Cell 51 compare with their earlier results.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. Reported without a pass/fail test.

64.found: Not run yet. No new question was written. The 11 questions, reports and one-word scoring are those of Cell 51. For the longer sections, the surrounding caveats are real specialist sentences from Cell 48, taken from the same scenario where it has enough. A trial run on a question Cell 51 had dropped worked for all six readers.
64.means: The results decide how the paper describes the caveats section: whether model readers in general act on it, whether that depends on being told to look, and whether it survives a section of realistic length. Whether people act on it stays open, since one person cannot run a reader study.

10285.label: Plan
10285.title: Six readers, a neutral instruction and longer sections
10285.summary: Each reader gets the report with no section, with Cell 51's one-sentence section, and, under an instruction that no longer mentions attachments, with sections of 1, 5 and 10 sentences. The relevant and irrelevant versions differ in one line. Five reads per setup on 11 questions, 550 reads per reader.

65.title: Do AI judges from other model families share the preference?
65.description: Four more AI judges compare the same 378 pairs of answers as Cell 43, in both orders, with the same instructions. Every pair counts, with a pair the judge calls differently in the two orders counting as half. Planned and queued to run.
65.size: Planned: 3,024 judgments by four added judges
65.why: Two judges have compared Cell 43's pairs: gpt-oss, which also wrote every answer, and qwen3-vl. Both preferred combined answers and marked down a scripted caveat phrase. A review in October 2026 asked whether that holds beyond those two. This cell adds Qwen2.5, Phi-4, Llama 3 and Mistral as judges. One of them, Qwen2.5, picked the first answer it read in 234 of its 240 earlier calls, so we set a rule in advance for leaving out a judge that only follows reading order.

expectations.text: Taken together, the added judges that count would prefer the combined answer to the single answer.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. This is the main expectation of the cell.

expectations.text: Taken together, the added judges that count would score the answer containing 'modeled at' below the plain answer.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. The cell has not run.

expectations.text: Taken together, the added judges that count would score the answer containing 'taken to be' below the plain answer.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. The cell has not run.

expectations.text: We would report each judge's wins, losses and split pairs, how often it picked the first answer it read, and how often judges agree with each other.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. Reported without a pass/fail test.

65.found: Not run yet. No answer is written for this cell. The pairs, the judge's instructions and the settings are those of Cell 43. A trial run on a made-up pair worked for all four judges. Three picked the better answer in both orders, and Qwen2.5 picked the first one it read both times.
65.means: If the added judges share the preferences, the paper can describe them as common to local AI judges of this size. If they do not, the two earlier results are properties of two particular judges. Either way the results say nothing about what people prefer.

10396.label: Plan
10396.title: Four more judges on the same 378 pairs
10396.summary: The four judges see each pair in both orders. A judge counts only if at most 20% of its pairs are unusable and it picked the first answer it read less than 95% of the time. For each comparison, the judges that count are averaged within each of the 18 scenarios and tested against an even split.

66.title: Are caveats lost more than ordinary sentences?
66.description: For 285 caveat sentences and 285 ordinary sentences of similar length, two AI judges decide whether each is conveyed in the editor's answer. The judging is done. Since the author cannot label 120 cases, the judges will be checked on public human labels instead.
66.size: AI judging done, a check on public labels queued
66.why: The editor's answer is about 30% as long as the specialists' text, so most sentences of any kind are left out. The corrected word-for-word figure of 3% (Cell 48) misses caveats restated in the editor's words, and the formula's share w (Cell 46) mostly reflects length. Neither says whether caveats are dropped more than other content. A review in October 2026 asked for that comparison. This cell makes it, and first checks the scoring against a person's labels.

expectations.text: The judges' rule would pass a check against human labels: at first the author's 120 blind labels, now 300 public human-labeled sentences plus 260 cases with a known answer.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. The replacement check was written down on 2 October 2026 and runs after the current queue.

expectations.text: Caveat sentences would be conveyed less often than ordinary sentences of similar length from the same text.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. This is the main expectation of the cell, and it could also come out even or the other way.

expectations.text: We would report how often caveats and ordinary sentences are conveyed fully or partly, and how often a judge reading the whole answer finds something the shortlist missed.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. Reported without a pass/fail test.

66.found: The two AI judges finished all 1,710 cases on 2 October 2026. The plan had the author label 120 cases blind to check the judges before the comparison could be read. That turned out not to be possible, so on the same day, before anything from the judges was read, we wrote down a replacement check and queued it. The judges will be scored on 300 human-labeled summary sentences from a public benchmark (FRANK), where people marked whether a sentence is supported by its article, with the same pass marks as before. They will also be scored on 260 cases with a known answer, built from answers the experiment does not use. Those are sentences copied from the answer itself, sentences with one figure changed by a fixed rule, and sentences from a different scenario. Only if that check passes will the comparison be read. Nothing about the comparison has been computed or shown.
66.means: If caveats are conveyed less often, the paper can say the editor drops caution in particular, and by how much. If they are conveyed about as often, the claim that prose loses caution is withdrawn in favor of a plainer one: the answer is shorter than its sources and keeps caveats in proportion.

10466.label: Plan
10466.title: Compare caveats with ordinary sentences of the same length
10466.summary: For each sentence, the three closest sentences in the editor's answer are found automatically, and two AI judges say whether its content is conveyed fully, partly or not. The author then labels 120 cases blind to check the judges. The main comparison is made within each of the 14 scenarios that have at least five caveats.

11083.label: Note
11083.title: AI judging finished, the comparison waits for labels
11083.summary: The two AI judges finished all 1,710 cases on 2 October 2026, and 120 of them were drawn for the author to label blind. No result of the comparison is computed or shown until those labels are finished and saved.

11097.label: Note
11097.title: The judging ran cleanly, and the 120 cases are ready to label
11097.summary: Both AI judges gave a readable answer for every one of the 1,710 cases, and the whole-answer check on 60 cases also finished. The 120 cases for the author were drawn by the rule written down in advance, and the answer key is kept apart from them. We have read nothing from the judges' answers. The step took 8.6 hours instead of the 7.7 planned.

11143.label: Change to the plan
11143.title: The author's labels replaced by public human labels and known answers
11143.summary: Written down on 2 October 2026 before anything from the judges was read. The 120 blind labels the author could not provide are replaced by two checks with the same pass marks. One uses 300 human-labeled summary sentences from the public FRANK benchmark, the other 260 cases with a known answer built from unused material. The comparison is read only if that check passes.

67.title: Does a second source help in the full live system?
67.description: The 61 computed-answer questions of Cell 63 go through the full live system. One specialist's private notes hold a wrong figure. In one version a second specialist's notes hold the right one. A script checks the final answer. Planned. It runs only if Cell 63's first check passes.
67.why: Cell 59 ran this design live on 8 questions and scored answers by matching figures in text. The editor used the second specialist's value, but whether the planted value appeared less often was too close to call. This cell repeats it on 61 questions where the final answer is a number a script can check, with both versions run in the same session. It is the first test of the assembled system on something other than AI judges' preference.

expectations.text: The wrong figure would show up in the first specialist's text, and the right one in the second specialist's text, in at least 75% of runs. Otherwise the rest cannot be read.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. In Cell 59 specialists passed on their figures in 85% to 95% of runs.

expectations.text: The final answer would follow the wrong figure less often when a second specialist holds the right one.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. This is the main expectation of the cell.

expectations.text: The final answer would be correct more often when a second specialist holds the right figure.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. The cell has not run.

expectations.text: When two specialists hold different figures, the final answer would mention both in fewer than half of runs.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. The cell has not run.

expectations.text: We would report what happens when both figures reach the specialists' texts, whether the editor's list of disagreements names both, and where the follow-up question goes.
expectations.note: Not tested yet. Reported without a pass/fail test.

67.found: Not run yet. A trial of the whole chain on a question outside the set took about ten minutes and returned a correct final answer. The planning step once used up its length allowance while thinking, as in Cell 61, so the short steps were given the larger allowance that Cell 61 ended with.
67.means: The results show whether giving a figure to a second specialist changes what the full system answers, and whether a disagreement between two specialists reaches the reader. The specialists here are the editor model in three roles, and the questions are arithmetic and rule questions, not the advisory scenarios.

10572.label: Plan
10572.title: The wrong figure through the full live system
10572.summary: The figure is removed from the scenario and reaches the system only through a specialist's private notes. Both versions share the same plan and the same texts from the two specialists whose notes do not change. One run per question and version, 61 pairs, scored by a script against the computed answers.

68.title: Is the pipeline better than asking one model four times?
68.description: A design for testing the project's first question on public questions where a single model is right about half the time, with four setups of equal cost. It is written down but not scheduled, because it needs public question sets to be downloaded.
68.why: The project began by asking whether a council of specialists answers better than one model. Three of our own question sets could not tell, because the single model was already right 92% to 98% of the time (Cells 36, 60 and 60-R). Every preference result also compared four model calls with one. A review in October 2026 named the missing comparison: the same model asked four times, with a vote. This entry fixes the design now so that later results cannot shape it.

expectations.text: The specialist pipeline would be more accurate than one direct answer from the same model.
expectations.note: Not tested. The cell is a design only.

expectations.text: The specialist pipeline would be more accurate than the same model asked four times with a majority vote.
expectations.note: Not tested. This comparison shows whether the specialist roles add anything.

expectations.text: The rebuilt system would be at least as accurate as the plain specialist pipeline.
expectations.note: Not tested. The cell is a design only.

68.found: Not run, and not scheduled. The design uses public questions with a single checkable answer in medicine, law and finance. It keeps only those the single model gets right two to four times in six, and compares four setups on the same questions in one session. Sizes would be fixed in a second entry once the questions are in hand.
68.means: Until this runs, the project has no evidence that the specialist roles add accuracy beyond asking one model several times. It needs the author's go-ahead to download public question sets.

10675.label: Plan
10675.title: A design for the first question, with room to improve
10675.summary: Public questions in three fields, screened so the single model is right about half the time. Four setups of equal cost: one answer, four answers with a vote, the specialist pipeline, and the rebuilt system. Scored by exact match. Written down now and not scheduled.

board-review.title: Outside-style review of the whole project
board-review.description: A review in October 2026 judged the paper not ready: several key numbers were wrong or overstated. We fixed one scoring bug, recomputed the small-sample results, withdrew or restated the affected claims, and planned seven new experiments.
board-review.size: No new runs, saved results recomputed
board-review.why: The paper had been drafted and three earlier audits had run. Before publication we asked for a review of everything: the question, the methods, each experiment, the notebook and the paper, set against published research. The reviewer was an AI assistant working from the project's files, as the earlier auditors were, so its report is a list of claims that can be checked, with a script that reproduces every number.
board-review.found:
The review did not accept the paper. It found a scoring bug behind one widely quoted number (17% of caveats surviving in the editor's prose, which is 3%). It found that ranges computed over 6 to 18 scenarios or questions were too narrow, and that preference results counted only about a third of the pairs. It found that the two AI judges' sentence labels agree little beyond chance. It also pointed out that in most experiments the three specialists are the editor model itself in three roles, that the paper's comparison is four model calls against one, and that no person labeled, judged or read anything.

Without any new model runs, we recomputed 14 results. Five statements survive with clear support. An instruction produces the phrase it names. AI judges prefer the combined answer and mark down the instructed phrase. A reader model acts on an appended sentence. And a second source changes which figure the editor repeats. One claim was withdrawn, that the editor ignores agreement between specialists.
board-review.means: The paper is being rewritten to claim only what the corrected numbers support, on one 20-billion-parameter model. Six new experiments are planned to run on one machine, and a seventh is written down as a design. Two of them need the author to label sentences by hand, because the project has no human labels at all. What one person cannot do stays open: a second person checking the analysis, human readers, and a much larger model.

entry-9592.label: Correction
entry-9592.title: What the review found and what we corrected
entry-9592.summary: The review's decision was major revision. This entry lists the corrected numbers in one table and the change of method behind them: averaging within each scenario or question first, and counting every pair. It also lists the five statements that survive and the seven experiments planned next, each with its own entry.

entry-10723.label: Plan
entry-10723.title: How the planned experiments are run and written down
entry-10723.summary: The six runnable experiments run back to back from one script. When a step ends, the script copies the scoring output into the notebook unedited, fills in the plain-language text from fixed templates, rebuilds this site and saves the changes locally. It never publishes. Results that could sway the author's blind labels stay hidden until those labels are saved.
